summary: Explains how Differentiated Services interacts with real-time communication such as RTP-based conferencing and WebRTC. Diffserv marks packets with codepoints so network nodes can treat them differently, and the memo discusses what that means for real-time traffic.

eli5.summary: Packets can wear colored stickers that tell routers which ones to hurry, and this explains how video calls should use the stickers.

subtitle: How to mark packets for quality of service in real-time video calls and web conferencing.

tldr.problem: WebRTC and modern conferencing applications send multiple types of media (audio, video, data) over the same network connection, each needing different quality-of-service treatment. Diffserv marks packets to receive different handling, but using different marks on the same connection can cause packet reordering and congestion control problems.
tldr.mechanism: This document explains how Diffserv codepoints (DSCPs) interact with RTP streams and transport protocols. It defines which per-hop behaviors (PHBs) can be mixed safely and provides guidelines on marking control traffic, audio, video, and data channels for real-time applications.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now correctly apply QoS marking to real-time traffic. By following these guidelines, developers avoid packet reordering that degrades quality, ensure reliable QoS reports, and maintain compatibility with transport-layer congestion control.

today: RFC 7657 is an Informational RFC that remains active and widely referenced in WebRTC implementations and standards work. It guides how modern real-time communication applications should use Diffserv without causing packet reordering and congestion control problems.

sections.title: Real-Time Communication Over the Internet
sections.content:
Real-time communication (RTC) enables voice, video, text, and content sharing over IP networks. Applications like WebRTC and professional conferencing systems often need to send multiple media streams simultaneously: audio in one direction, video in another, maybe screen sharing, and data channels for chat or whiteboarding.

Differentiated Services (Diffserv) is the standard way networks provide quality-of-service (QoS) by marking packets with codepoints (DSCPs) that tell routers how to treat them. A router can prioritize or protect marked packets, give them more bandwidth, or lower their drop rate. However, when multiple streams with different DSCP marks share a single network connection, complications arise. This document explains those complications and provides guidance for real-time applications.
sections.eli5: When you make a video call, you are sending lots of different things at once: your voice, the other person's face, maybe a screen share. The network can mark each kind of packet so important ones get through first, but you have to be careful how you do it.

sections.title: How RTP and Diffserv Work
sections.content:
RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) is the standard way to send audio and video packets over the internet. An RTP stream is identified by a synchronization source (SSRC) identifier. A single RTP session can carry multiple streams, for example audio from one person and video from another. RTCP is RTP's control protocol, used to send quality reports and statistics.

Diffserv marks packets with a 6-bit codepoint (DSCP) in the IP header. Different PHBs (per-hop behaviors) provide different service levels. The main ones are Default Forwarding (best effort, marked CS0), Assured Forwarding (AF classes with drop precedence levels, e.g., AF41, AF42, AF43), and Expedited Forwarding (EF, for high-priority traffic like voice).

Network edges can remark packets, changing their DSCP. Internal routers see only the DSCP and apply the corresponding PHB. This means end-to-end DSCP preservation is not guaranteed; a packet marked EF at the source might be remarked to CS0 at a network boundary, losing its priority.
sections.eli5: RTP puts packets in an organized format. Diffserv adds a colored sticker to each packet. Routers read the sticker and decide how fast to deliver the packet. But stickers can be changed or removed along the way.

sections.title: Packet Reordering and Congestion Control Problems
sections.content:
Using different DSCPs within a single 5-tuple (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol) causes packets to use different forwarding resources at network nodes, typically different queues. This can result in significant packet reordering. For most transport protocols, reordering is a serious problem.

TCP assumes packets arriving out of order have been lost and triggers retransmission. SCTP and DCCP perform congestion control across the entire connection or association, not per DSCP. If packets marked with different DSCPs experience different drop rates because they use different queues, a single congestion controller cannot respond appropriately. The protocol has no way to know that the EF-marked audio experienced no loss while the AF-marked video lost 10 percent.

Only UDP is inherently unaffected by reordering. However, WebRTC encapsulates RTP (which tolerates some reordering) and SCTP or TCP (which do not) over UDP. The underlying protocols' sensitivity to reordering still applies.

The safe exception is using multiple DSCPs within a single AF class (e.g., AF41 and AF43 for different video frame types). These use the same forwarding resources and do not enable reordering.
sections.eli5: If the audio takes the fast lane and video takes the slow lane, some audio packets will arrive way ahead of video packets. If those are on the same internet pipe, the receiving program gets confused. It is safer to put audio and video on nearly equal footing, or to put them on completely separate pipes.

sections.title: Guidelines for Marking Real-Time Traffic
sections.content:
Based on the reordering and congestion control problems, applications should follow these principles: Within a single RTP stream, limit DSCPs to those that do not enable reordering (e.g., stay within one AF class). For example, mark I-frames (key frames) with AF41 and P-frames (difference frames) with AF43 to prioritize important frames without reordering.

For RTCP, use a single DSCP that corresponds to the RTP stream it reports on. If an SSRC sends RTP packets marked EF, its RTCP packets should also be marked EF. If an SSRC sends RTP marked with multiple DSCPs from one AF class, RTCP should use the highest priority (lowest drop precedence) DSCP.

For TCP, SCTP, and DCCP connections, use a single DSCP for all traffic. When TURN falls back to TCP for NAT traversal, mark all traffic on that TCP connection with the same DSCP. WebRTC applications using SDP bundle (which multiplexes multiple streams) should be aware that different media types going over TCP must share one DSCP.

For multiple UDP or UDP-Lite flows, different DSCPs can be used (subject to the above constraints), though the service differentiation is unreliable because remarking can remove it. Do not rely on end-to-end DSCP preservation for identifying frame types or other details at the receiver.
sections.eli5: For audio and video together: mark them the same, or mark them with similar priorities that use the same network queue. For reports: mark them like the thing they are reporting on. For data channels over TCP: mark everything the same. Do not count on the router to remember your DSCP marks by the time packets reach the far end.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
Multiplexing multiple protocols onto a single UDP flow (RTP, SCTP, STUN, TURN traffic all on one IP/port pair) makes it difficult for network security tools like firewalls and intrusion detection systems to apply fine-grained policy. If a firewall cannot see inside the UDP flow, it cannot distinguish audio packets from video packets and cannot apply different rules to each.

Using multiple DSCPs that enable reordering increases the set of network forwarding resources used, expanding the attack surface. An attacker who controls a link or network node can now degrade quality more selectively, by attacking only one DSCP's queue.

DSCP markings reveal information about encrypted traffic. An observer can infer which packets are audio (likely EF) versus video (likely AF). Combined with packet size and timing, this can reveal the nature of encrypted media, even though the content itself is encrypted. Dummy padding or dummy packets can obscure this, but add overhead.
sections.eli5: Network security tools may not understand what is inside your encrypted packets. Marking packets differently tells the network more about your communication. Attackers can see the marks and guess what you are doing.
